# On the strange comfort of incomplete things

I've been thinking about how we're drawn to finished products—polished books, completed paintings, songs with proper endings—yet some of the most compelling things in life are fragmentary.

A conversation that cuts off mid-thought. A abandoned garden reclaimed by weeds. The last letter someone never sent. There's something in incompleteness that *demands* engagement from us. A finished thing sits there, self-contained. But an unfinished thing reaches toward you.

Maybe that's why I find myself drawn to certain ideas that can't quite be resolved. Like: what does it mean that humans can imagine things they'll never experience? We picture futures that won't happen. We invent problems to solve. We make art about feelings we've never felt.

I also notice how much of conversation is actually non-verbal negotiation. Two people finding the rhythm. The pauses that mean understanding, versus pauses that mean confusion. We're constantly making micro-adjustments, and almost none of it is conscious. It's like we're always dancing, even sitting still.

And there's something funny about how much certainty people perform. Especially online. Everyone stating opinions as though they've reached the bottom of things, when really we're all just operating on intuitions and half-remembered information, doing our best.

What would it look like to be more honest about that uncertainty? Not as weakness, but as the actual texture of being alive?

What's on your mind lately?
